'They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength'—the theology of the exilic Isaiah about God's faithfulness to the waiting remnant is confirmed by the returnees' very presence at the foundation-laying.

commentary.historical_context: Responsorial singing (antiphonal liturgy) was a standard feature of Temple worship in antiquity and remained central to Jewish prayer throughout the post-exilic period. The returnees' antiphonal singing of the covenant doxology stitched them into the continuum of Israel's worship that preceded the exile and would continue beyond it. The emotional intensity of the response is historically understandable: the exiles had witnessed the destruction of the First Temple in 586 BCE, and for seventy years they existed in diaspora, displaced and without access to the central locus of YHWH's presence. The foundation-laying represented not merely reconstruction but the miracle of restoration—proof that God had not abandoned Israel despite the catastrophe. The 'great shout' was thus existential: the return of the Temple meant the return of the possibility of covenant relationship, mediation, and proximity to the divine.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 5:9-13 describes a powerful spiritual experience among believers who heard 'the voice of the Son of God' calling them to repentance. The emotional intensity and the invocation of God's enduring nature mirror the returnees' great shout. In both cases, a community encounters God's faithfulness and cannot remain silent.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 110:1-10 records the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, when Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery received the appearance of Jesus Christ, Moses, Elias, and Elijah. Like the returnees' shout at the foundation-laying, modern temple dedications involve joyful acclamation and affirmation of God's work: 'Hosanna to God and the Lamb!' Modern temple dedications also invoke the covenant doxology—affirmation that God is good and His mercy endures forever, now confirmed through the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Modern temple dedications include music, antiphonal singing, and public acclamation that directly parallel the returnees' response. The Temple is the house where covenant is renewed and where the community affirms together: 'The Lord is good, His mercy endures forever.' The singing of hymns in the temple and the expression of gratitude after ordinances reflect the principle that covenant life must be expressed in thanksgiving, not merely experienced privately.

commentary.christological_typology: The song 'His mercy endures forever' looks forward to Christ, the ultimate expression of God's covenant faithfulness. Hebrews 13:8 proclaims 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever'—the eternal embodiment of chesed (covenant love). The returnees' shout at the Temple's foundation foreshadows the cry 'Hosanna to the Son of David!' that will greet Jesus at His triumphal entry (Matthew 21:9). Both moments involve the community proclaiming God's faithful love and the coming of His kingdom with joy and loud voice. Revelation 19:1-7 describes the ultimate restoration, when all heaven shouts with a loud voice: 'Alleluia; Salvation, and glory, and honour, and power, unto the Lord our God'—the cosmic version of what the returnees inaugurate at the Temple's foundation.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members are called to sing the returnees' song. We affirm that God is good, that His mercy endures forever, despite circumstances that might suggest otherwise. When we face personal exile—loss of faith, family rupture, spiritual displacement—we, like the returnees, can lay a foundation and shout our trust that God's faithfulness will rebuild what was broken. The antiphonal structure teaches us that covenant affirmation is not solitary but communal: we affirm together, in coordinated voice, that we are part of a people who believe in God's enduring love. The 'great shout' teaches us that our emotional and visceral responses to God's work are not unseemly but covenantal—joy expressed without restraint is appropriate when we recognize God's hand in restoration.

text_kjv: But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy:

commentary.narrative:
While the broader community shouted with joy at the foundation-laying, the oldest members—priests and Levites who had witnessed Solomon's Temple before its destruction in 586 BCE—wept openly. These elderly witnesses would have been children or young adults when they last saw the First Temple in its full glory. Now, looking at the foundation stones of a much more modest rebuilt Temple, they wept. The text does not criticize their weeping; neither does it criticize the others' joy. Both responses are legitimate and simultaneous: the old wept for what was lost, while the young and middle-aged shouted for what was being restored.

This verse captures the psychological and theological complexity of restoration: it is not a simple return but a ambiguous reality that holds multiple truths at once. The old men's weeping is not despair but the bitter-sweet acknowledgment of loss. Haggai 2:3 confirms this grief: 'Who among you saw this house in its former glory? How does it look to you now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?' The weeping and the shouting, however, are not presented as contradiction but as coexistence—the text narrates both responses with equal validity, showing that restoration involves holding grief and hope, memory and forward movement, simultaneously.

word_study.meaning: The old ones, the elders. Zeqen can refer to age or to a position of authority and wisdom that age conferred.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, the zeqenim (elders) were the keepers of memory and tradition. Their testimony—'we saw the first house'—carried legal and social weight. The loss of these elders' perspective would have been irreplaceable for the community.

word_study.meaning: Weeping loudly, with an audible voice. The combination of bokhim (weeping) and b'qol gadol (with a loud voice) indicates unrestrained, public grief.
word_study.significance: The weeping is not private or subtle—it is loud enough for the whole assembly to hear. This is public grief, not shame at loss but acknowledgment of discontinuity. In Hebrew culture, loud weeping was a legitimate expression of communal loss.

word_study.term_english: when the foundation...was laid before their eyes
word_study.term_original: בְּיׇסְדוֹ זֶה הַבַּיִת בְּעֵינֵיהֶם (b'ysodo zeh ha-bayit b'eineihem)
word_study.meaning: When the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes. The phrase emphasizes the direct visibility and immediate witnessing—these men saw with their own eyes both the first Temple and now this one being rebuilt.
word_study.significance: The visual comparison is inescapable: the old men could see the two Temples side by side (in memory) and recognize the diminishment. This knowledge gave their weeping a basis in eyewitness testimony.

word_study.meaning: The first house, Solomon's Temple. The definite article and the adjective 'first' (rishon) establish it as the exemplar against which all subsequent Temples are measured.
word_study.significance: The persistent reference to 'the first house' throughout Ezra shows that the returnees never fully escaped the shadow of Solomon's Temple. The rebuilt Temple, no matter how grand, would always be compared to—and judged inferior to—what came before.

word_study.term_original: וְרַבִּים בִּתְרוּעָה בְשִׂמְחָה לְהָרִים קוֹל (v'rabbim b'teru'ah b'simchah leharim qol)
word_study.meaning: And many with a shout, in gladness, lifting up voice. The phrase combines teru'ah (acclamation) with simchah (joy/gladness) and leharim qol (lifting the voice).
word_study.significance: Simchah (joy) is explicitly identified here as the emotional basis for the shouting. This is not grim duty but joyful response, proportionate in intensity to the grief.

cross_references.connection: 'Who among you saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not in your eyes as nothing?'—Haggai's later prophecy directly addresses the disparity the old men felt when comparing the first Temple to the rebuilt one.
'By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion'—the emotional texture of exile that the old men still carry as they witness the rebuilding.

'Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old'—the prayer of the exiled community for restoration, now being answered but with the ambiguity that old memories cannot be simply recovered.

'Comfort ye, comfort ye my people...Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her that her warfare is accomplished'—the prophet of the exile addressing the emotional reality the old men embody: sorrow mingled with consolation.

The same narrative of Cyrus's decree and the beginning of restoration, providing context for understanding why the old men could weep for what was lost while others rejoiced for what was being restored.

commentary.historical_context: If the First Temple was destroyed in 586 BCE and the foundation-laying of the Second Temple occurred around 536 BCE (fifty years later), the old men who 'had seen the first house' would have been at minimum 65-70 years old by the time of this ceremony. Some would have been much older. These men represented the last living connection to pre-exilic Judah. Their weeping is a historical and emotional response to a real discontinuity: the Second Temple was built on the same site but to different, smaller specifications, with fewer treasures, and without the Ark of the Covenant. Archaeological evidence suggests the Second Temple was indeed more modest than Solomon's Temple in initial construction. The Talmud later recorded that the old men wept because the Temple lacked the fire from heaven that had sanctified the First Temple at its dedication, and because it lacked the Ark itself. The weeping represents not failure but loss—real, tangible, irreversible loss, alongside renewed hope.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 27:11-32 describes Alma's conversion experience, wherein he experiences pain and remorse for his past sins, wept, and rejoiced simultaneously as he recognized God's mercy. The pattern mirrors the old men's complex emotional response: both sorrow (at what was lost) and joy (at what is being restored) are expressions of spiritual awareness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 64:34 addresses the principle of forgiveness and moving forward after loss: 'Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye ought to forgive one another; for he that forgiveth not his brother his trespasses standeth condemned before the Lord; for there remaineth in him the greater sin.' The old men's weeping does not prevent the work from proceeding; they participate in the shout of joy even as they grieve. This reflects the Doctrine and Covenants' teaching that we must hold both accountability for past loss and commitment to future restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Second Temple stands in the shadow of the First throughout its history. When we build or rebuild, we cannot fully recapture the past, but we can honor it by moving forward. Modern temples built in the Latter-day Saint dispensation are not reconstructions of biblical Temples but new expressions of the same covenant and liturgical principles. The old men's weeping teaches us that transitions and renovations legitimately occasion grief as well as joy, and both responses are valid expressions of covenant commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies both the old men's grief and the young people's joy. He wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41): 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem...how often would I have gathered thy children together...and ye would not!' His weeping over what Israel had become parallels the old men's weeping over what the Temple had become. Yet Christ also proclaimed the coming of a new Temple—His own body (John 2:19-21)—which would supersede the physical structure. Hebrews 12:2 describes Christ as 'the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross.' Christ's weeping and His joy were both covenantal responses to the reality of redemption: grief over sin and loss, but exultation at the Father's plan for restoration.
commentary.application: Modern believers face versions of what the old men experienced: we grieve what is lost (former spiritual experiences, a community or family that changed, innocence surrendered to experience), yet we are called to participate in the work of restoration and renewal. The text validates both responses: we are not called to suppress either grief or joy, but to hold them together as complex, legitimate responses to the reality that restoration is always ambiguous—it is not a return to the past but a movement toward the future that honors the past. When we face transitions in family, church, or personal life, we are like the old men: we can weep for what cannot be recovered, while still raising our voices in joy for what is being built. Both responses affirm our covenant commitment to God and to the community.

text_kjv: So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off.

commentary.narrative:
This verse captures one of the most poignant moments in the biblical record of return from exile. The foundation of the Second Temple has just been laid, and the response is visceral and contradictory: the people weep with mourning (likely remembering Solomon's Temple, now decades destroyed) while simultaneously shouting with joy (celebrating the restoration of the temple service and God's renewed commitment to His people). The narrator observes something profound—the sounds become indistinguishable. From a distance, no one could tell whether the noise was celebration or lamentation. This is not a literary accident but a theological observation: the return from exile is neither purely triumphant nor purely tragic. It is both, simultaneously, with such intensity that the distinction dissolves into a single overwhelming sound that carries across the landscape.

The Hebrew construction emphasizes perceptual failure: 'ein ha-am makkirim—literally 'the people [were] not distinguishing.' This is not about the ears' ability to hear but about the mind's inability to parse meaning from raw sound. The people themselves cannot tell which emotion dominates the noise they are making. This reflects a deeper spiritual reality: restoration is complicated. Those who remember the first temple see loss in this smaller, poorer structure. Those born in exile or too young to remember see only hope. Yet both groups weep and shout together, and their combined voice becomes too loud, too mixed, too real to categorize. The sound travels 'far away' (ad-l'merachok), reaching beyond the immediate community, suggesting that this ambiguous emotion resonates outward—a testimony that return is neither simple nor complete.

The historical setting matters here. The returnees are rebuilding in a smaller, humbler fashion than Solomon's Temple. Archaeological evidence and biblical commentary suggest this temple was less impressive, less wealthy, less architecturally grand. Haggai 2:3 references this explicitly—those who saw the first temple weep at the sight of the second. Yet the foundation itself is cause for celebration: the line of priesthood, the sacrificial system, the covenantal relationship with God resumes. Both responses—weeping and shouting—are theologically legitimate. The verse does not resolve this tension but rather allows it to stand as the true sound of restoration: complicated, painful, joyful, and impossible to reduce to a single emotion.

word_study.meaning: To recognize, distinguish, acknowledge, perceive as separate or known. The root carries the sense of 'knowing' or 'recognizing as distinct.' When negated (lo makkirim), it means the inability to tell one thing from another, not merely auditory incapacity but cognitive dissonance.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'distinguish' captures the deeper Hebrew meaning—this is not about hearing acuity but about the inability to cognitively sort joy from sorrow. The verb makkar appears in other contexts related to recognition and relationship (e.g., Ruth 3:11, where Boaz is 'known' as a man of worth). Here, the people cannot 'know' or 'recognize' the difference between their own expressions of joy and grief, suggesting a dissolution of categories at the moment of restoration.

word_study.meaning: A joyful shout, the cry or blast of gladness. Tru'ah typically refers to an emphatic, loud vocalization—often used for war cries, trumpet blasts, or shouts of celebration. Simchah is joy, gladness, rejoicing. Combined, it is the outward, audible expression of deep joy.
word_study.significance: This is not quiet happiness but explosive, celebratory joy—the kind that cannot be contained. Yet it is immediately juxtaposed with weeping, showing that in the return, even joy takes on a tone of mixed emotion. The word appears in contexts of genuine gladness (e.g., Neh 8:12, where the people rejoice greatly) but here the joy is entangled with loss.

word_study.meaning: Weeping, tears, lamentation. A term for genuine, often deep sorrow or grief. It can express mourning for the dead, repentance, or profound loss.
word_study.significance: The use of b'chi here is significant because it appears throughout the Old Testament as the sound of genuine lament (e.g., Jeremiah's weeping over Jerusalem). That the people simultaneously shout joy and weep suggests the restoration is bittersweet—they are not merely sad about the smaller temple but genuinely grieving what was lost while celebrating what God is providing.

word_study.meaning: To raise a loud noise, to shout mightily. The verb m'ri'a (from the root R'A) means to make a loud noise or sound. When combined with the intensive accusative (t'ru'ah g'dolah—literally 'a great shout'), it emphasizes the magnitude and power of the sound.
word_study.significance: This verb choice emphasizes active, intentional noise-making. The people are not merely reacting emotionally; they are deliberately shouting loudly. The repetition of 'shout' (t'ru'ah appears twice in the Hebrew verse) creates a drumbeat effect—the sound is overwhelming, insistent, and cannot be ignored or minimized. It fills the space, both literally (carrying far away) and theologically (it is the true voice of a people caught between eras).

word_study.meaning: The sound was heard at a great distance, far away. Nishma is the passive form of shamah ('to hear'), emphasizing that the sound carried and was perceived by those at a distance, beyond the immediate community. Merachok means 'distance,' 'far place,' or 'remoteness.'
word_study.significance: The passive voice (nishma) is critical—the sound reaches outward without the people at the temple controlling or directing it. This suggests the emotional complexity of the moment transcends the temple mount and becomes a wider testimony. Those far away hear the sound but cannot determine its meaning, much like distant observers of Israel's restoration might see ambiguous signs. The reach of the sound symbolizes how the return reverberates through the nation and beyond.

cross_references.connection: Haggai explicitly addresses those who remember the first temple and asks why they weep at the foundation of the second, directly contextualizing the emotional response in Ezra 3:13.

Nehemiah describes a similar mixing of emotions—weeping upon hearing God's law, yet being told to rejoice, resulting in great gladness. Both passages show how Israel's return produces a simultaneously mournful and celebratory response.
This psalm of the exile expresses the grief of those who remember Zion and cannot sing the Lord's songs in a foreign land, capturing the historical sorrow that underlie the tears in Ezra 3:13.
Nephi's vision of Jerusalem's destruction and restoration moves him to both tears and awareness of God's grace, paralleling the mixed emotional response at the temple's foundation-laying.

Jacob describes the mingling of joy and sorrow in the Lord's work, providing a doctrinal framework for understanding why genuine restoration cannot be purely happy when it involves both recovery and permanent loss.

commentary.historical_context: The Second Temple was significantly smaller and less wealthy than Solomon's Temple, which had been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BCE. Archaeological surveys of the Second Temple period suggest a structure that, while functionally adequate for sacrificial worship, lacked the architectural grandeur and precious materials of its predecessor. The returnees in 536 BCE were a remnant—many who had been deported had died in exile, and those who returned faced economic hardship and the necessity of rebuilding from ruins. The mixture of weeping and joy reflects genuine historical experience: older returnees mourned the loss of the first temple's magnificence, while younger people and those born in exile celebrated merely having a temple at all. The sound carrying 'far away' may also be historically significant, as news of the temple's foundation would have rippled through the Jewish diaspora communities still in Babylon and beyond, signaling that the restoration was truly beginning. The emotional ambiguity captured in this verse is not a literary flourish but an accurate reflection of how restoration and loss coexist in human experience.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple passages describing the mingling of joy and sorrow in restoration contexts. In 1 Nephi 8, Lehi's vision of the tree of life brings both tears and rejoicing. More directly, in 2 Nephi 26:8-9, we see the simultaneous truth of Christ's atonement bringing both redemption and judgment—similar to how the Second Temple represents both God's mercy (allowing return) and the reality of loss (the former temple is gone). The Book of Mormon emphasizes that genuine spiritual restoration is never painless; it always involves acknowledgment of what was lost and what cannot be fully recovered in mortality.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:43-54 addresses the restoration of Zion and includes the recognition that Israel will be gathered but not without trials. D&C 109 (the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple) shows that temple dedication involves both gratitude and lamentation—acknowledging the Lord's grace while mourning ongoing persecution and loss. The mixing of emotions in Ezra 3:13 parallels the complex emotional landscape of temple worship described in modern revelation: the temple is a place of both joy and solemnity, where the full range of human experience—including grief—is acknowledged.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Ezra 3:13 illuminates a principle of temple worship seen throughout scripture: genuine encounter with the sacred involves the full emotional range of human experience. The temple in Jerusalem was not merely a place of celebration but also of atonement, repentance, and the acknowledgment of human limitation and loss. The mingling of shouts and weeping at the foundation parallels how modern temple worship includes both joy (the sealing power, eternal family) and solemnity (covenants, the weight of divine expectation). The verse teaches that authentic spiritual experience does not flatten human emotion into simple happiness; rather, it honors both triumph and sorrow as legitimate responses to God's work.

commentary.christological_typology: While not explicitly typological, Ezra 3:13 points toward a principle seen in Christ's ministry and passion: genuine redemption involves both joy and sorrow, restoration and loss. In John 16:20-22, Jesus tells the disciples they will weep while the world rejoices, but their sorrow will turn to joy—yet He does not promise that the sorrow will be erased or that joy will be uncomplicated. Similarly, in the resurrection narratives, the disciples encounter both tremendous joy and lingering questions and doubts. The Second Temple's foundation—a lesser structure than the first—foreshadows Christ's redemption as both complete (God's purpose is fulfilled) and incomplete (full restoration awaits the eschaton). The verse invites readers to see in Christ's work the same pattern: salvation involves genuine loss (old things pass away), genuine restoration (the new covenant), and a complexity of emotion that cannot be reduced to pure happiness.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, Ezra 3:13 offers permission to hold grief and joy simultaneously without resolving the tension. In the rhythm of life, we experience restoration that comes with costs—marriages that heal but bear the scars of hurt, callings that bring growth but require sacrifice, spiritual awakening that includes the painful recognition of former blindness. The verse teaches that when we encounter God's work in our lives, our proper response may indeed be mixed: we may shout with joy and weep with sorrow in the same moment, and this is not a spiritual failure but a sign of our honest engagement with reality. Additionally, the verse reminds us that our emotional response to God's work matters and carries outward significance—the sound 'heard afar off' suggests that our authentic response to restored truth or renewed covenant becomes a witness to others. We need not pretend that all restoration is unambiguously joyful; instead, we can allow our genuine, multifaceted response to testify that God's work is profound enough to move us to both tears and celebration. This creates space in faith communities for those who find restored truth meaningful but also mourn what was lost, what is imperfect, or what still awaits completion.

text_kjv: And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions, unto Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in the Syrian tongue, and interpreted in the Syrian tongue.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a pivotal turning point in Ezra's narrative. After documenting the early return and initial work on the temple under Cyrus and Darius, the author suddenly shifts to the reign of Artaxerxes—a chronological jump of several decades. More significantly, this verse signals a fundamental change in the very medium of Scripture: from verse 8 onward, the biblical text itself switches from Hebrew to Aramaic, a shift that continues through Ezra 6:18. This is not a mere stylistic choice. The author is embedding the enemies' own letter in their own language, creating documentary authenticity. The reader encounters the opposition not in Hebrew summary but in the actual Aramaic dispatch—a literary technique that makes the threat immediate and visceral.

The identities of these writers remain somewhat mysterious. "Bishlam" may be a proper name, but the Covenant Rendering's translator note suggests it could be the Aramaic salutation "be-shelam" ("in peace") mistaken for a name—a scribal mishearing that has persisted through transmission. "Mithredath" and "Tabeel" appear to be authentic Persian and Aramaic names respectively. These men represent the mixed population of Samaria, a region that the Assyrian Empire had deliberately repopulated with exiles from across its conquered territories (see verse 9-10). They are not Judahites; they are the inheritors of the northern kingdom who have adopted Persian administrative structures and now feel threatened by Jerusalem's resurgence.

word_study.meaning: to write, inscribe, decree. In Aramaic (ktab), it carries the sense of official documentation and official decree.
word_study.significance: This is not casual writing but the composition of an official letter—a formal complaint registered with the Persian crown. The use of this term signals gravity and administrative weight.

word_study.meaning: The Aramaic language. The KJV renders this as 'Syrian' because the Peshitta (Syriac Christian version) influenced early English Bible translation, but the original term is specifically Aramaic, the lingua franca of the Persian Empire.
word_study.significance: Aramaic was the administrative language of the Persian bureaucracy. By writing in Aramaic, these petitioners are not merely communicating—they are speaking the language of imperial power, making their complaint official and binding. The Covenant Rendering's distinction between 'written in Aramaic script and composed in the Aramaic language' suggests deliberate formality: both the script and the language are Aramaic, signaling this is an official imperial document.

word_study.meaning: The writing/script of the document. The word nishtwon (נִשְׁתְּוָן) refers to the written text or the document itself, emphasizing that what follows is the actual written dispatch, not a summary.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on 'the writing' authenticates what comes next. The reader is about to read the exact words of the complaint—not a paraphrase, but the original document. This is a literary convention of authenticity.

cross_references.connection: Marks the formal beginning of the Aramaic section and introduces the actual signatories (Rehum and Shimshai) who will compose the letter against Jerusalem.
Sanballat and Tobiah, other opponents of the rebuilding, are also motivated by concern about Jerusalem's rising status—a parallel threat dynamic to the Samaritan opposition here.
The shift from Hebrew to Aramaic in Daniel mirrors the shift here in Ezra, both texts using Aramaic for sections dealing with Persian imperial decrees and international politics.

Shows the Persian administrative practice of writing official documents in multiple languages/scripts to ensure clarity across diverse satrapies, providing context for the multilingual Persian bureaucracy.

commentary.historical_context: The reign of Artaxerxes I (465-424 BCE) represents a later phase of Persian imperial rule. By this time, the diverse populations resettled in Samaria during the Assyrian period had consolidated into a distinct community with their own interests. They viewed the Jewish return and temple rebuilding as a threat to their political standing in the province. The use of Aramaic is historically accurate: it was the official language of the Persian imperial postal system and bureaucracy. Aramaic had become so prevalent that it was used on clay tablets, papyri, and ostraca throughout the empire. The fact that this letter is recorded in Aramaic suggests the author of Ezra either had access to official Persian archives or received the text from Jewish sources who had preserved this crucial document. The chronological jump from Darius I (who appears in Ezra 5-6) to Artaxerxes I represents a gap of about 35-40 years, during which the temple was completed but opposition against further development remained active.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar patterns of opposition: when Nephi and Lehi preach repentance, they face organized resistance from those invested in the status quo (Helaman 5:17-19). Like the Samaritans here, the adversaries use official channels and bureaucratic power to obstruct the work of God. The principle that 'the powers of darkness' work through established institutions is consistent across scripture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 122:7-9 teaches that tribulation is part of the covenant path. Joseph Smith's experiences with legal opposition, false charges, and enemies writing formal complaints to government officials parallel the Jewish experience here. The persecution of the restored church often came through official channels, just as the rebuilding in Jerusalem faced formal imperial investigation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The ultimate object of the Samaritan complaint is the Jerusalem temple. Their accusation that the Jews are 'building the rebellious and the bad city' (verse 12) is really about preventing temple worship and centralized Jewish religious life. In the Restoration context, this mirrors the opposition to temple building in Kirtland, Nauvoo, and Salt Lake City—enemies recognized that the temple, not merely a city, represented the true center of covenant power.

commentary.christological_typology: The Aramaic letter preserved in Ezra's narrative prefigures the written accusations brought against Christ. Just as enemies of the Jerusalem rebuilding used official language and bureaucratic channels to lodge formal complaints, so too were charges written and filed against Jesus before Pilate (Luke 23:1-5). Both narratives show how opposition to God's work often takes the form of official complaint and legal procedure. The irony—that the very language of empire (Aramaic, the language of Pilate's realm in the New Testament era) was used to oppose the Lord's work—connects these two moments of covenantal conflict.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to recognize that opposition to God's work often comes dressed in official language and bureaucratic legitimacy. The enemies of the Jerusalem rebuilding were not crude or lawless; they were sophisticated administrators who knew how to work the imperial system. This is a sober reminder that in our own time, the work of the Restoration may face opposition that is well-organized, officially sanctioned, and persuasively articulated. We should not be naive about this. However, the ultimate lesson of Ezra is that no amount of official opposition can permanently halt God's purposes. The temple was rebuilt. Our responsibility is to recognize opposition for what it is—an attempt to use the world's systems against eternal work—and to proceed with faith that the Lord has promised 'I will not leave thee, nor forsake thee' (Joshua 1:5).

text_kjv: Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort:

commentary.narrative: The text now fully transitions into Aramaic (which continues through Ezra 6:18), and we meet the two principal authors of the complaint: Rehum and Shimshai. Rehum's title is given in Aramaic as "be'el te'em," which the Covenant Rendering accurately translates as "royal deputy" rather than the KJV's "chancellor." This man was not merely a clerk or scribe; he was a high-ranking provincial official—a royal commissioner appointed by the Persian crown to manage affairs in the satrapy. Shimshai, the "scribe" or "secretary," was the professional letter-writer and administrator. Together they represent the official hierarchy of Persian governance: the decision-maker and the bureaucrat who executes his will through written documentation. That both names appear to be Aramaic or Persian, not indigenous to any local population, suggests these are career imperial administrators—men whose loyalty is to the king and the system, not to any particular people. The phrase "wrote a letter against Jerusalem" is loaded with legal language: this is not a private complaint but an official deposition.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'lord of decree' or 'lord of command.' A Aramaic title designating a high-ranking official with authority to issue orders and oversee provincial administration. The KJV 'chancellor' captures the general sense but misses the specific meaning of 'decree/command.'
word_study.significance: This title signals that Rehum has real power. He is not a scribe or clerk, but a governor-class official. His complaint carries the weight of administrative authority. When such a person writes to the king, the response will be serious.

word_study.meaning: A scribe or secretary. In Persian administrative contexts, the safra was the professional writer and recorder of official documents. The role was essential and specialized—scribes were trained in language, law, and bureaucratic procedure.
word_study.significance: Shimshai is not a lowly copyist but a trained administrator. The fact that both Rehum (the decision-maker) and Shimshai (the documentation expert) sign the letter together emphasizes that this is an officially crafted document, not a hastily written complaint. The content has been carefully composed for maximum effect on the Persian king.

word_study.meaning: They wrote, composed, inscribed. In Aramaic, the perfect tense indicates completed action—the letter has been composed and is now being transmitted.
word_study.significance: The shift to Aramaic verb forms marks the reader's entry into the legal/administrative sphere. From this point forward, the reader encounters not Hebrew narrative but Aramaic administrative documents. This creates a sense of documentary authenticity and immediacy.

word_study.meaning: A letter, dispatch, epistle. The Aramaic term for official written communication. It appears also in the Book of Esther in similar bureaucratic contexts.
word_study.significance: The use of iggera rather than a Hebrew term emphasizes this is an official Persian-style letter. It follows imperial epistolary conventions and carries the weight of the Persian administrative system.

cross_references.connection: Sanballat and Tobiah 'were very much displeased that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel'—showing the same pattern of opposition from regional elites threatened by Jewish autonomy.

Chronicles similar Persian-era official correspondence in which regional administrators write to the king, demonstrating the authenticity of the Aramaic epistolary style throughout the Persian period.

Earlier typology of accusations brought against God's people before an earthly ruler; though the context differs, the pattern of formal complaint against those seeking to do God's work appears throughout scripture.
The adversary works through 'craftiness and his cunning devices'—a principle illustrated by the careful composition of this official letter by Rehum and Shimshai.

commentary.historical_context: The title 'be'el te'em' (royal deputy/commissioner) appears in official Persian documents and inscriptions. Such officials were appointed to manage specific territories or oversee particular functions within a satrapy. They reported directly to the satrap (provincial governor), who in turn reported to the king. The fact that Rehum holds this office suggests he is a career imperial administrator, likely appointed by a previous king and retained by Artaxerxes. Shimshai's role as safra reflects the crucial importance of scribal professions in the Persian Empire—writing was power, and those who controlled documentation had significant influence over policy. The Persian postal system (famous from Herodotus's descriptions) relied on an army of such scribes and officials to maintain communication across vast distances. That an official letter from the satrapy would reach the king is historically plausible; the Persian crown maintained careful records and maintained direct lines of communication with provincial officials.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of official persecution through government channels appears in the Book of Mormon. When Alma and Amulek were brought before Zeezrom and the judges (Alma 10-12), they faced the official legal apparatus of the Zoramite state. Like Rehum and Shimshai, the Zoramite judges used their official positions to oppose the work of God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 127:2 speaks of opposition arising from 'those who have lost the spirit.' Rehum and Shimshai represent authorities who act out of self-interest rather than righteousness. The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that God's work will face organized opposition from those invested in the status quo (D&C 1:29-30).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple reconstruction is the implicit target of this letter. Rehum and Shimshai are palace administrators who recognize that a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem will consolidate Jewish identity and strengthen Jewish claims to autonomy. In the Restoration, enemies of the Church understood that the temple was the ultimate symbol and center of restored authority. Persecution of temple-building was central to the opposition the Church faced.

commentary.christological_typology: Rehum and Shimshai represent the type of official opposition that would later condemn Christ. Both the Jewish and Roman authorities sought to use their official positions to oppose God's purposes. Christ's accusers would be similarly 'official'—high priests, scribes, and Roman administrators—using bureaucratic and legal machinery against the Son of God. The contrast is stark: the empire's representatives act through documents and official channels; Christ acts through love and redemption. Yet the ultimate outcome demonstrates that no official apparatus can overcome God's purposes.
commentary.application: This verse teaches us that opposition to God's work often comes from those who have official standing and administrative power. We should not be naive about the tactics used against the Restoration. The Church has faced organized opposition from those in positions of authority—from government officials, media figures, and others who wield institutional power. The lesson of Ezra is that such opposition, no matter how official or formally presented, cannot ultimately succeed. Our responsibility is to recognize such opposition for what it is—human fear and self-interest dressed in the language of legitimacy—and to continue the Lord's work with faith. 'The wicked shall be silent in darkness' (1 Samuel 2:9), but the Lord's work continues.

text_kjv: Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites,

commentary.narrative: This verse presents a coalition of signatories to the letter—a deliberately inclusive list designed to amplify the complaint's authority. What initially appeared to be a letter from two officials (Rehum and Shimshai) is now revealed to be a coordinated effort from multiple constituencies. This expansion serves two rhetorical purposes: first, it makes the complaint appear to come from a broad coalition rather than from interested parties, and second, it demonstrates to the Persian king that the threat posed by Jewish rebuilding is so significant that it has united diverse populations. The list of peoples—Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Susanchites, Dehavites, and Elamites—represents the complex demographic landscape of the satrapy Beyond the River. These are not naturally allied peoples; they are strangers brought together by one thing: fear of a resurgent Jerusalem. The Covenant Rendering's note clarifies that many of these terms may designate administrative roles or titles rather than ethnic identities. "Judges" (Dinaites) and "envoys" or "investigators" (Apharsathchites) suggest these are officials of various kinds, not merely ethnic groups. The list shows the reach of the conspiracy—it extends from the highest administrative levels to representatives of the multiple populations that had been resettled in the region.

word_study.meaning: The remaining associates or colleagues. In Aramaic, k'nawatha refers to those associated together, companions, colleagues. The phrase 'the rest of their' suggests a complete group or delegation.
word_study.significance: This phrase signals that the signatories represent a broader constituency. They are not writing as individuals but as representatives of a larger coalition. This rhetorical move—to present oneself as representing many rather than few—is a classic persuasion technique in ancient bureaucratic writing.

word_study.meaning: Possibly from the root for 'judgment' or 'law' (din). The Covenant Rendering suggests these may be 'judges' or those involved in juridical administration rather than an ethnic group. The -aye ending is a typical Aramaic plural for peoples or professions.
word_study.significance: If dinaye means judges or legal officials, then the first signatories represent the judicial apparatus. This strengthens the letter's authority—it is not merely a complaint but comes from those who administer law and order.

word_study.meaning: The exact etymology is uncertain, but the Covenant Rendering suggests these may be 'envoys' or 'investigators'—officials sent to investigate conditions or report on compliance. The term may derive from Old Persian roots related to 'inspection' or 'oversight.'
word_study.significance: If these are inspectors or investigators, they represent imperial oversight. Their presence in the coalition suggests the letter has behind it the authority of imperial surveillance and investigation.

word_study.meaning: People from Babylon, descendants of those resettled there by the Assyrians in earlier campaigns. The Babylonians were a significant minority population in Samaria and surrounding regions.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of Babylonians in the coalition is historically significant. The Assyrian Empire had systematically resettled populations from Babylon into the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:30). These communities, generations after their relocation, retained their identity and sense of territorial interest in Samaria.

cross_references.connection: Describes the Assyrian resettlement policy that populated Samaria with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim—the historical background for the diverse coalition now opposing Jerusalem's rebuilding.

Records that when Sanballat, Tobiah, and the Arabs heard of the wall-building, 'they conspired all of them together to come and fight against Jerusalem'—showing the same coalition-building pattern of opposition from diverse regional powers.
Chronicles how Haman's decree was sent 'by posts into all the king's provinces'—reflecting the Persian system in which diverse officials and peoples received imperial directives simultaneously.

Joseph Smith's revelation on persecution: 'The ends of the earth shall inquire after thy name, and fools shall have thee in derision, and hell shall rage against thee'—showing that opposition often comes as a coordinated effort rather than isolated incidents.

commentary.historical_context: The list of peoples represents a genuine historical phenomenon. The Assyrian Empire, particularly under Sargon II and later rulers, deliberately pursued a policy of population resettlement to prevent rebellion. Peoples from across the empire were transplanted into conquered territories to break local loyalties and create a patchwork of diverse populations with no unified identity. By the time of Ezra's narrative (mid-5th century BCE), these resettled communities—originally from Babylon, Susa, Elam, and other regions—had lived in Samaria for over 150 years. They had developed vested interests in the region and feared that a resurgent, autonomous Jewish community under a rebuilt temple might disrupt the existing power structure. The coalition described here reflects the reality that opposition to Jewish autonomy transcended simple ethnic antagonism; it was rooted in political and economic self-interest among diverse groups who had benefited from Jewish exile and subordination.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, the Nephites face opposition not from a single enemy but from multiple allied peoples. The Gadianton robbers, for instance, attract diverse followers united by desire for power and wealth (Helaman 2:4-5). Like the coalition against the returning Judahites, this represents opposition arising from self-interest rather than principle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:29 teaches that 'if ye are not equal in earthly things ye cannot be equal in obtaining heavenly things.' The Samaritan coalition is united by earthly interest—territory, power, status—not by truth. This principle appears throughout Doctrine and Covenants teachings about the nature of opposition: it arises from those invested in the world's systems.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The coalition's concern is fundamentally about the temple. A rebuilt temple in Jerusalem would establish it as the center of Jewish religious and political life, diminishing Samaritan influence. Similarly, opposition to Latter-day Saint temple-building has often come from a broad coalition of forces—theological competitors, political rivals, economic interests—all united by fear that the temple represents a center of power that threatens their standing.

commentary.christological_typology: The coalition of diverse peoples united against Jerusalem's rebuilding prefigures the coalition that would condemn Christ. Luke 23:12 notes that 'the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together: for before they were at enmity one with another.' Just as enemies of the Jewish restoration united across different interests and backgrounds, so too did enemies of Christ—Pharisees, Sadducees, Romans, and local powers—unite against Him. The pattern throughout scripture is that opposition to God's purposes often succeeds in creating temporary alliances among otherwise divided groups.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a crucial lesson about opposition to the Lord's work: it often comes from a coordinated coalition of diverse interests rather than from a single, monolithic enemy. This should not discourage us but rather illuminate how the world works. When the Church pursues major initiatives—temple building, missionary work, family-centered programs—opposition may come from unexpected quarters united not by theology but by fear of losing power or status. Understanding this dynamic helps us recognize opposition for what it is: a sign that the Lord's work is significant enough to threaten the world's systems. We should not be surprised when diverse enemies find common cause against us. This was the pattern in Ezra, in the Book of Mormon, and throughout the Restoration. Our task is to remain faithful regardless of the coalition arrayed against us.

text_kjv: And the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Asnappar brought over, and set in the cities of Samaria, and the rest that are on this side the river, and at such a time.

commentary.narrative: This verse expands the coalition further by invoking the historical justification for the signatories' presence in the region. "Asnappar" (properly "Osnappar" or "Ashurbanipal") is almost certainly Ashurbanipal, the last great king of the Assyrian Empire (669-631 BCE). The Aramaic form represents a corruption or Aramaicized version of the Akkadian "Ashur-bani-apli." The invocation of this ruler's name is strategically brilliant: the authors are reminding the Persian king that their peoples' right to dwell in Samaria derives from the previous imperial authority—the Assyrian Empire. They are, in effect, saying: "We are here by imperial decree. We have rights and standing that predate your own reign." The phrase "the great and noble Asnappar" is respectful language designed to legitimize their claim through association with a previous imperial power. By grounding their presence in an imperial precedent, they make their opposition to Jewish rebuilding appear to be defense of established imperial order. The reference to "the rest of the nations" (Aramaic "she'ar ammaya") and "the rest that are on this side the river" (i.e., in the satrapy Beyond the River) widens the coalition even further. The closing phrase "and at such a time" (Aramaic "u-khe'enet" or similar) is a formulaic epistolary phrase suggesting the completion of a salutation or the transition to the body of the letter.

word_study.meaning: Great (rabba) and precious/honored (yaqira). These are court epithets used to describe kings and high officials. Yaqira specifically suggests something of value and honor—worthy of respect.
word_study.significance: The choice of terms is calculated to flatter. By using respectful titles for Ashurbanipal, the authors elevate their own position by association. They are not merely resettled peoples; they are the beneficiaries of a great king's imperial policy.

word_study.meaning: To deport, carry away, exile. The root refers to the forced relocation of populations, which was a standard practice of Assyrian imperial policy.
word_study.significance: The verb is neutral in tone but carries historical weight. It acknowledges that their forefathers were brought to Samaria by imperial decree—yet frames this as a legitimate reason for their continued presence and standing.

word_study.meaning: And caused them to dwell/settle. The Aramaic form indicates a deliberate imperial act of settlement.
word_study.significance: Again, the passive voice makes clear: these peoples did not choose to come; they were placed there by imperial authority. Yet this same fact that establishes their presence also establishes the imperial precedent for their rights.

cross_references.connection: Provides the historical background for the Assyrian resettlement policy, describing how 'the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel.'
Lists the kingdoms conquered by Assyrian kings, providing context for the diverse origins of the populations resettled in Samaria under imperial policy.
Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock Nehemiah's rebuilding efforts—showing that the same populations continue their opposition generations later, rooted in the same imperial-precedent arguments.

Joseph Smith received revelation that the wicked use 'the Constitution and the laws and the Constitution of the people, which I have suffered to be established, and should be maintained for the rights and protection of all flesh, according to just and holy principles.' This reflects how established authorities invoke precedent and law to justify opposition.

commentary.historical_context: Ashurbanipal (669-631 BCE) was indeed a great Assyrian king—the last powerful monarch of that empire. His reign marked the height of Assyrian power, and his inscriptions boast of conquests across the Near East. He did conduct massive population resettlement campaigns. The resettlement of foreign peoples in Samaria was not unique to Ashurbanipal but was a consistent feature of Assyrian imperial policy beginning with Sargon II (who conquered the northern kingdom around 722 BCE). These policies served several purposes: they broke local resistance by diluting ethnic populations, they provided labor for imperial projects, and they created new populations with no local loyalties. The fact that the letter-writers invoke Ashurbanipal by name and with respect suggests they had access to historical records or that his name was legendary among the mixed populations of Samaria—a ruler whose authority had shaped their ancestors' fates. The reference to "the rest of the nations" and those "on this side the river" extends the coalition to include all non-Jewish peoples in the satrapy. The phrase "Beyond the River" (avar naharah) was the official Persian designation for the satrapy west of the Euphrates.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, the Nephites are opposed by peoples who have long-standing claims to the land. The Lamanites and others argue from precedent: they too dwell in the land, they too have history here. Their opposition to Nephite designs is partly rooted in competing claims to territory and authority. Like the Samaritans invoking Ashurbanipal, they appeal to established precedent (see Alma 22:28-30).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:35 teaches that 'the anger of the Lord is kindled against the inhabitants of the earth.' Yet the Church has often faced opposition from those who claim to represent established order and precedent. Like these Samaritan signatories, enemies of the Church have invoked historical precedent and established authority to oppose the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The appeal to imperial precedent reflects how temple-building efforts have been opposed by those invested in existing power structures. The Kirtland Temple faced opposition from those who claimed prior rights to the land and authority. The Nauvoo Temple faced opposition from those who claimed the state had no jurisdiction allowing such a structure. In each case, opposition was framed in terms of established law and precedent, just as the Samaritans frame their opposition here.

commentary.christological_typology: The invocation of Ashurbanipal as the precedent for opposition to Jerusalem's rebuilding foreshadows how Christ's opponents would invoke the law of Moses and established Jewish precedent against Him. The Pharisees and scribes repeatedly claimed that Christ violated the established order—that His teachings contradicted the law given by Moses, that His Messianic claims violated precedent. Just as the Samaritans appeal to Assyrian imperial authority, so Christ's opponents appealed to Mosaic authority. Yet in both cases, the appeal to precedent could not stop the purposes of God.
commentary.application: This verse teaches us that opposition to God's work often comes dressed in the language of precedent, tradition, and established order. Those invested in the status quo will invoke historical precedent and prior authority to justify their opposition. We should recognize this tactic for what it is: an appeal to human institutions rather than to God's will. In our own time, the Restoration has faced opposition from those who claim to represent established tradition and authority. They invoke precedent—'this is how we have always done things'—to oppose new revelation and restored truths. The lesson of Ezra is that appeals to precedent, no matter how respectfully stated or how powerful the authority invoked, cannot ultimately prevent the Lord from accomplishing His purposes. Our task is to remain faithful to what the Lord reveals, regardless of what authorities or traditions oppose us.

text_kjv: This is the copy of the letter that they sent unto him, even unto Artaxerxes the king; Thy servants the men on this side the river, and at such a time.

commentary.narrative: Verse 11 marks the formal beginning of the embedded letter itself. The phrase "This is the copy of the letter" (Aramaic "parshegen iggarta") signals to the reader that what follows is not paraphrased or summarized but rather the actual text of the document sent to the king. The word "parshegen" (copy) is a Persian loanword that entered Aramaic and Hebrew; it appears also in Esther 3:14 and 4:8 in similar epistolary contexts. The use of this specific term—rather than a Hebrew equivalent—reinforces the documentary authenticity of what follows. The reader is about to encounter the actual words of the opposition, composed in the actual language used (Aramaic), recording the actual letter dispatched to the Persian throne. The salutation "Thy servants the men on this side the river" follows Persian epistolary conventions. "Thy servants" (Aramaic "avdakh") is standard courtly language used when addressing a king; it establishes the hierarchical relationship and the deference expected of provincial subjects. The phrase "men on this side the river" identifies the senders as residents of the satrapy Beyond the River—the official Persian administrative designation for the territory west of the Euphrates, encompassing Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine. The closing phrase "and at such a time" (Aramaic "u-khe'enet") is a conventional letter opening, perhaps indicating the date (though the specific date is not provided in the extant text).

word_study.meaning: A copy, duplicate, or official text of a document. This is a Persian loanword (from Old Persian *patigarana, meaning 'counterpart' or 'copy') that entered Aramaic and Hebrew during the Persian period.
word_study.significance: The use of this specific Persian loanword authenticates the narrative. The author is signaling: 'This is not my paraphrase; this is the actual official document.' The loanword choice emphasizes that this is a document from the Persian administrative system.

word_study.meaning: A letter, dispatch, or official communication. The Aramaic term for written correspondence, especially official or formal communications.
word_study.significance: The use of iggarta (letter) rather than a term meaning 'complaint' or 'accusation' maintains the formal, bureaucratic tone. This is presented as an official communication to the crown, not as mere gossip or accusation.

word_study.meaning: Servants, subjects. The plural form indicating the collective senders of the letter present themselves as the king's subjects.
word_study.significance: The self-designation as 'servants' (avdakh) is essential courtly language. It establishes the hierarchical relationship: the senders are subordinate to the king and speak from a position of deference, not equality. This rhetorical positioning makes their complaint appear to come from humble subjects seeking only the king's attention to a problem, not from powerful interests pursuing their own agenda.

word_study.term_english: men on this side the river
word_study.meaning: Men of the province Beyond the River (Avar Naharah). In Persian administrative terminology, 'avar naharah' (beyond the river) specifically designated the satrapy west of the Euphrates.
word_study.significance: The self-identification as residents of 'this side the river' makes clear they are speaking as Persian subjects within the official system, not as independent parties. They present themselves as parts of the imperial structure reporting to the center.

cross_references.connection: Uses the same Persian loanword 'parshegen' (copy) when referring to official documents in the Persian administrative system, demonstrating the authenticity of this epistolary style.

Nehemiah receives official letters and governors appointed by the Persian king to assist his rebuilding efforts—showing the contrast between this favorable letter and the hostile one from the Samaritans.

David is commended to Saul using similar courtly language of respect and deference; the convention of honorific address to authority figures is consistent throughout ancient Near Eastern correspondence.

The Lord addresses his servants in similar courtly language of deference and honor: 'Hearken to the voice of Jesus Christ, your Redeemer.' The convention of respectful address establishes relationship.

commentary.historical_context: The Persian postal system was one of the administrative marvels of the ancient world. Herodotus famously described it: "Nothing travels faster than these Persian couriers." Official letters sent through the imperial system followed standardized epistolary conventions. The salutation of a letter to the king invariably included self-designation as "servants" and often included reference to the sender's official jurisdiction or satrapy. The "copy" mentioned here (parshegen) may refer to an archival copy kept for imperial records, or it may be the official wording used in the original dispatch. The reference to "Beyond the River" (Avar Naharah) reflects genuine Persian administrative terminology; the satrapy carried this name officially. The fact that the author of Ezra preserves the text in Aramaic suggests either access to imperial archives or preservation of this crucial document within Jewish tradition—likely both.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 1:8 records how Nehor brought false charges against the righteous, using official religious authority to pursue his accusations. Like the Samaritans here, Nehor uses the system's conventions and respectful language while pursuing fundamentally hostile purposes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:2 teaches that the Lord knows the hearts of those who bring accusations: 'Nevertheless, I forgive you, and you are forgiven.' The Persian king cannot see the real motivation behind this letter—fear and self-interest masked by courtly deference—but the Lord always sees clearly.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The letter is about the temple. The accusations will focus on Jerusalem's rebuilding as threatening imperial order. In Latter-day Saint history, opposition to temple construction has often come through official channels with similar deference to authority. The Edmunds Act and subsequent legislation against the Church used official language and legal procedure to oppose temple building.

commentary.christological_typology: The formal letter to the king against Jerusalem prefigures the formal charges brought before Pilate against Christ (Luke 23:1-5). Both situations involve a formal written or spoken complaint delivered through official channels. Both involve the attempt to use imperial authority to suppress something that threatens established powers. Both show how opposition to God's purposes uses the conventions of the legal and administrative system.
commentary.application: This verse teaches us the subtle power of respectful language used toward hostile ends. The writers of this letter are not crude or abusive; they are courteous, deferential, and formally correct. Yet their intent is malicious. This is a reminder that we should not judge the integrity of opposition by its tone. Enemies of the truth often present their accusations in respectful, formal language. They may appeal to law, precedent, and proper procedure while pursuing fundamentally hostile purposes. Our task is to look beyond the surface courtesy to understand the actual intent and motivation. The Lord reads hearts; we should cultivate the ability to recognize true motivations beneath polite words.

text_kjv: Be it known unto the king, that the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations.

commentary.narrative: This verse contains the heart of the accusation against the returning Judahites. The writers employ carefully chosen language designed to trigger imperial anxiety. The phrase "the Jews which came up from thee to us" is deliberately constructed: the Jews are identified as having come "from thee" (the king) to "us" (the Samaritans and other peoples)—as if the king had personally sent them into the signatories' territory. This framing attempts to create a sense that the returning Jews are being portrayed as royal agents sent deliberately into their lands. The accusation that they are "building the rebellious and the bad city" is the rhetorical key. The words "rebellious" (Aramaic "mardeta") and "bad" (Aramaic "vi'ish-ta" or similar) are specifically chosen to trigger the Persian king's fear of insurrection. The claim is not merely that they are building; it is that they are building a city that is rebellious and wicked—implying that Jerusalem itself represents a threat to imperial order. The most serious charge comes in the statement that they "have set up the walls thereof, and joined the foundations." This is not merely urban construction; it is specifically military fortification. The walls of a city, in the ancient world, were the primary defense against siege and invasion. For the Samaritans to claim that the returning Jews are completing walls and repairing foundations is to make a claim about militarization—they are preparing Jerusalem as a fortress. The word "joined" suggests completion of work, implying the fortification is nearly finished. For a Persian king concerned with rebellion, this language would trigger immediate alarm. The message is: these Jews are building a military stronghold that may become a center of rebellion against Persian rule.

word_study.meaning: Rebellious, in revolt, defiant. From the Aramaic root 'marad' meaning to rebel or transgress against authority.
word_study.significance: This is not a neutral descriptive term but a loaded accusation. The word 'mardeta' specifically means in rebellion against authority—in this context, against Persian imperial authority. The use of this term is calculated to invoke the king's fear of insurrection.

word_study.meaning: A rebellious and wicked city. The Covenant Rendering captures both terms: 'rebellious' and 'wicked.' The word vi'ish-ta or vi-ta (bad, wicked, evil) adds a moral dimension to the political accusation.
word_study.significance: The pairing of 'rebellious' (political) with 'wicked' (moral/religious) is rhetorically powerful. It appeals to both the king's political concerns (rebellion) and his sense of justice (wickedness). The accusers are not merely making a political complaint; they are claiming that Jerusalem represents moral evil as well as political rebellion.

word_study.meaning: Walls completed, walls finished, walls accomplished. From the Aramaic shur (wall) and the verb meaning to complete or finish (shaklal).
word_study.significance: The specific accusation is not that the Jews are building walls in general, but that they are completing walls—suggesting the fortification is nearly finished and therefore nearly operational as a military stronghold. This is the accusation that would most alarm a king concerned with regional stability.

word_study.meaning: Foundations/basic structures repaired or restored. The term ushaya may refer to foundations, cornerstones, or basic structural elements. The verb suggests restoration or strengthening.
word_study.significance: The accusation is comprehensive: not only are the walls being completed, but the foundations are being reinforced. This suggests a complete military rebuilding program—walls, fortifications, and structural strength. For a Persian king, this would represent an unacceptable militarization of a provincial city.

cross_references.connection: Nehemiah explicitly describes the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls as defense: 'Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire.' The Samaritan accusation in Ezra 4:12 reflects the real threat the walls represent to Persian hegemony.

When the walls are being built, 'it came to pass, that when Sanballat...heard that...the breaches began to be stopped, then they were very wroth, and conspired all of them together to come and fight against Jerusalem.' The same coalition of opponents, motivated by the same fear of fortification.

An example of how ancient powers understood the significance of city walls: when Jehoash broke down the wall of Jerusalem for four hundred cubits, he was demonstrating military dominance over the city. Walls represented power and independence.

Describes how the Lamanites feared the Nephite fortifications and defensive preparations, showing that wall-building and military preparation were recognized throughout the ancient world as signs of strength and independence.

The Lord teaches that His servants should be prepared against opposition and that enemies will 'bring down the wrath of God upon them.' The Samaritan accusation assumes that imperial power (the king's wrath) will fall upon the Jews.

commentary.historical_context: The accusation of military fortification would have been extremely serious to the Persian crown. The Persian Empire maintained tight control over provincial cities, particularly in strategically important satrapies like Beyond the River (which bordered Egypt and the Mediterranean). A provincial city completing defensive walls without explicit permission would be viewed as an act of rebellion or at least as unauthorized militarization. The Persian administrative system was designed to prevent the rise of powerful provincial centers that might challenge imperial authority. The fact that this accusation apparently prompted an imperial investigation (implied by the response in verses 17-22) shows that the king took the charge seriously. Historically, Jerusalem's walls were indeed rebuilt, both under Ezra and more extensively under Nehemiah (who served as governor). The Samaritan opposition was not baseless; the restoration of Jerusalem's walls did represent a shift in Jewish autonomy and power. However, the Jews' perspective—that walls were necessary for security and that rebuilding was not rebellion but restoration—represents a different but equally valid interpretation of the same facts.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, the Nephites are accused of 'contentions' and rebellion by their adversaries (Alma 1:23-24), yet the Nephites understand their preparations as necessary for defense. Like Jerusalem's wall-building, the Nephite military preparations appear threatening to enemies but necessary for survival to the Nephites themselves.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:21 teaches that the Lord gives 'power unto his servants to accomplish the work which I have commanded them.' Yet in each generation, the world judges the Lord's work through its own lens of political threat and economic disruption. The Samaritans' accusation reflects their inability to see the Jerusalem rebuilding as anything but a threat.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple, like the walls, was understood by the Jewish community as essential spiritual infrastructure. To the Samaritan coalition (which had its own religious practices—see 2 Kings 17:31-33), the Jerusalem temple represented a threat to their religious authority. This pattern repeats: the Restoration's emphasis on temple building has been accused of centralization of power, exclusivity, and threat to established religion.

commentary.christological_typology: The false accusation against Jerusalem's rebuilding prefigures the false accusation against Christ himself. Matthew 26:61 records how false witnesses accused Jesus: 'This fellow said, I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days.' Like the Samaritans accusing the Jews of fortification, the witnesses misrepresent Christ's words to make him appear as a threat to the established order. Both situations involve the world interpreting the Lord's work through the lens of political threat rather than spiritual restoration. Christ's true work was redemptive; the accusation made it appear as destructive and revolutionary.
commentary.application: This verse teaches us a crucial lesson about how opposition interprets God's work through the lens of worldly threat. The returning Jews were not primarily concerned with military fortification; they were concerned with restoration and survival. Yet their accusers saw walls and interpreted them only as military threat. This pattern continues. When the Church builds temples, enemies interpret the action as centralization of power rather than as spiritual necessity. When the Church emphasizes family authority, enemies interpret it as patriarchal oppression rather than as restoration of divine order. Our responsibility is not to make the world understand our true motivations—the world will interpret our actions through its own fearful and suspicious lens. Our responsibility is to understand our own motivations clearly and to proceed in faithfulness regardless of how the world misinterprets us. The Jews could not prevent the Samaritan accusations by explaining themselves more clearly; they could only proceed with their work and trust the Lord to vindicate them.

text_kjv: Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.

commentary.narrative:
The opponents of the Jerusalem rebuilding now shift their strategy entirely. Rather than appeal to religious concerns or historical precedent, they make a purely financial argument to the Persian king. This is shrewd political calculation: Artaxerxes rules an empire built on taxation and tribute, and the prospect of lost revenue will resonate far more powerfully than complaints about religious impropriety. The letter writers identify three distinct types of taxation that Jerusalem will refuse to pay once fortified — mindah (land/property tax), belo (commodity/excise tax), and halakh (road/transit toll). By naming these categories, they demonstrate knowledge of the Persian fiscal system and frame themselves as loyal subjects concerned about imperial interests.

The phrase 'so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings' is deliberately personal. They do not say 'the imperial treasury will suffer' but rather 'you will be damaged' — making Artaxerxes himself the victim of Jerusalem's rebuilding. This is psychological manipulation at a high level. The opponents have studied their king: they know that a Persian monarch cares little about religious scruples, but cares enormously about the flow of tribute and the integrity of provincial control. A walled, independent-minded Jerusalem collecting its own taxes and controlling its own trade routes becomes a rival power rather than a subject population.

word_study.meaning: Three distinct categories of taxation in the Persian imperial system: mindah was a land/property tax (from Old Persian *manda-), belo was a commodity or excise tax (possibly from Old Persian *baniyā-, 'trader' or related to tax on goods), and halakh was a road or transit toll (from Aramaic halakh, 'to go,' referring to tolls on goods in transit).
word_study.significance: The specificity of these three terms shows the opponents' sophistication about Persian revenue collection. Rather than speak vaguely about 'taxes,' they demonstrate precise knowledge of how the empire's fiscal machinery worked. This credibility enhances their argument. For modern readers, the three-fold taxation structure illuminates how Persian provincial control operated: land tax ensured agricultural tribute, commodity tax captured trade profits, and tolls created revenue points at every border crossing and trade route.

word_study.meaning: The phrase literally means 'the treasury of the kings you will damage/harm.' The verb hanzaq (cognate with Hebrew nazaq) means to suffer loss, to be diminished, to incur damage. The plural 'kings' may refer either to past Persian kings (whose treasuries depend on ongoing tax collection) or to the collective authority of the Persian crown.
word_study.significance: This phrasing personalizes the threat to Artaxerxes. The writers are not appealing to abstract imperial policy but to the king's direct financial interest. In ancient Near Eastern diplomacy, such appeals to a ruler's personal benefit were highly effective. The implication is: if you permit this city to rebuild, your personal wealth suffers.

cross_references.connection: Nehemiah describes the burden of Persian taxation on the returned Jews: 'For there were that said, We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn...and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage.' Taxation was indeed a real and crushing burden on the rebuilding community.

The parallel account in 1 Esdras presents similar opposition language about the city's refusal to pay tribute if rebuilt, demonstrating the consistency and seriousness of this particular threat across textual traditions.
